name: Procore
tagline: Cloud construction management platform for RFIs, submittals, drawings, daily logs, budgets and field coordination across everyone on a job.

pricing.basis: annual contract, quoted against construction volume
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Procore does not publish list pricing and sells annual contracts sized to a company's construction volume.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely build a project tracker with RFIs, submittals, punch lists and daily logs in a weekend, and for a solo builder or a one-crew remodeler that is genuinely enough. But Procore is not a tracker, it is the shared record that a general contractor, twelve subs, an architect, an owner and an insurer all agree to look at. The value lives in the fact that everyone else is already in it, that the drawing markup and the RFI thread are admissible when the dispute happens, and that the accounting integration means budget numbers are not retyped. A personal replacement drops the moment you need a sub to log in and answer something. If you are one person on your own jobs, build it; if you are coordinating other companies, you are buying the coordination, not the forms.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you log daily site reports with photos, track RFIs and punch list items to closure, and export a dated PDF record per project.
requirements: local disk for photo storage (originals get large fast)
a phone browser for field entry, since there is no native app
optional: object storage if you want photos off one machine
whatYouLose: External parties: subs, architects and owners cannot log in, comment, or be held to a timestamped response
Drawing management: sheet versioning, overlays, hyperlinked details and markup that survives a revision set
The audit trail people actually litigate with, plus retention and permission controls that hold up under scrutiny
Financial plumbing: budget vs committed vs actual, change orders, and the accounting integrations that keep them in sync
Offline-first mobile capture, and the fact that a field crew will actually use it
moatNotes: The buyer is the GC but the users are everyone else on the job, which is why nobody rips it out mid-project.
whyPeopleStillPay: Construction runs on who said what and when, and Procore is the agreed-upon place that answer lives. Once the subs are trained, the drawing sets are uploaded, and the accounting system is wired in, switching mid-project is a risk nobody wants to own. The contract price is unpleasant and everyone complains about it, but the alternative is email threads and a shared folder, which is how claims get lost. You are paying for a neutral shared system of record with enough weight behind it that the other companies on the job will accept it.
notes: The forms are a weekend; the agreement that everyone uses the same forms is not. The moat is multi-company coordination plus a defensible audit trail, not the feature list.
prompt:
Build a local-first construction job log called "Sitebook". One person, own jobs, no other companies logging in.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind. No component library.
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/sitebook.db, schema created on boot if missing.
- Photo uploads written to ./data/uploads, served through a route handler. Generate a max-1600px web version with sharp, keep the original.
- PDF export with pdf-kit. Server-side only.
- No auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no third-party APIs. Binds to localhost by default; read PORT and optional BASIC_AUTH_USER / BASIC_AUTH_PASS from .env, ship .env.example.

Data model:
- Project: name, address, client, start date, status (active/closed).
- DailyLog: project, date, weather text, crew count, hours, work performed (markdown), delays/issues, photos (many).
- RFI: project, number (auto per project), subject, question, asked date, needed-by date, answer, answered date, status derived (open/answered/overdue).
- PunchItem: project, location, description, trade, photos, created date, due date, closed date, status derived.
- Attachment: parent type + id, filename, mime, bytes, caption.

Screens:
- Project list, then a project dashboard: open RFIs, overdue RFIs, open punch items, last 7 daily logs.
- Daily log form built for a phone: date defaults to today, drag or camera photo input, autosave draft to localStorage.
- RFI table and punch list table, both filterable by status and sortable by due date. Inline close/answer without a page reload.
- Per-project "Record" button: generates a PDF with a cover page, chronological daily logs with embedded photos and captions, an RFI register table, and a punch list table. Filename includes project slug and generation date.

Also: full-text search across daily log text, RFI subjects and punch descriptions using SQLite FTS5. A "Backup" button that zips data/ and streams it to the browser. Seed script with one fake project, 10 daily logs, 6 RFIs, 12 punch items.

Out of scope, do not build: budgets, change orders, drawing sheet versioning or markup, subcontractor invites, email notifications, offline sync, native apps.

Deliver a README with setup, how to run it on a phone over the LAN, where the data lives, and a blunt note that this is a single-operator log with no audit guarantees and no way for other parties to participate.
